study.title: The Major Scale Recipe
study.question: How is a major scale built?
study.passage:
Keyboard guide (written for this lesson):
On a keyboard, the white keys are C D E F G A B C. Black keys sit between most white keys.
Half steps: neighbouring keys with nothing between them, such as E–F and B–C (no black key between), or C–C♯.
Whole steps: two half steps, such as C–D (with C♯ between).
Major scale pattern: W W H W W W H.
C major: C–D (W), D–E (W), E–F (H), F–G (W), G–A (W), A–B (W), B–C (H). All white keys.
G major: G–A (W), A–B (W), B–C (H), C–D (W), D–E (W), E–F♯ (W), F♯–G (H). It needs F♯.
Solfège: do re mi fa so la ti do.
Activities: 1. Find half and whole steps on a keyboard. 2. Play C major. 3. Build G major and discover the F♯. 4. Build D major and find its two sharps (F♯, C♯). 5. Sing each scale with solfège.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; scale patterns follow standard music theory.

study.title: The Three-Chord Toolkit
study.question: How are chords built, and why are I, IV and V so important?
study.passage:
Chord guide (written for this lesson):
Build a triad: start on a root, skip a note, add the next, skip again, add the next. C triad = C (skip D) E (skip F) G.
In C major: I = C E G (C major); IV = F A C (F major); V = G B D (G major).
In G major: I = G B D; IV = C E G; V = D F♯ A.
Why these three? Together they contain every note of the scale, so they can accompany most melodies in that key. The V chord pulls strongly back to I.
Activities: 1. Build triads on every note of C major. 2. Play I–IV–V–I in C on keyboards (right hand) or ukuleles (C, F, G chords). 3. Hear the "pull": play I–IV–V and stop. Does it feel finished? Then play I. 4. Try inversions: C E G, E G C, G C E. Which is smoothest moving from C to F?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; chord construction follows standard music theory.

body.hook: Give a singer a melody and a guitarist three chords, and you have a band. Accompanying means choosing the right chord at the right moment so the melody sounds full and supported.

study.title: Back the Melody
study.question: How do I choose and play chords that fit a melody?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Matching chords (10 minutes): For each melody note in C major, find which primary chord contains it: C is in I and IV; D is in V; E is in I; F is in IV; G is in I and V; A is in IV; B is in V. On strong beats, choose a chord that contains the melody note.
2. Chord chart (10 minutes): "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" in C: | C | C | F | C | F | C | G | C |. Play one chord per bar while a partner sings or plays the melody.
3. Patterns (10 minutes): Keyboard: block chord on beat 1, or broken chord (root, fifth, third, fifth). Ukulele: down, down-up, down, down-up.
4. Your turn (15 minutes): In pairs, use chord tones to write a chord chart for "Mary Had a Little Lamb" in C using only I and V, then perform it.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; the melodies are traditional.
